title: Ham and Mustard Sandwich
subtitle: Thick-cut ham on white bread with English mustard
excerpt: Good thick-cut cooked ham between two slices of white bread with English mustard. The simplest and best of the British sandwich canon, dependent almost entirely on the quality of the ham.
sourceNotes: The British sandwich tradition dates from the eighteenth century, traditionally attributed to John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich (1718-1792). Ham and mustard as a sandwich filling is documented in British catering and cookbooks from the Victorian era onwards. The ploughman's lunch tradition, of which ham sandwiches are a part, is documented as a working British meal from at least the nineteenth century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble up to 2 hours ahead and wrap tightly in wax paper or cling film. Do not add mustard too far ahead or it will soak the bread.

content.text: A ham and mustard sandwich has four components: bread, butter, ham, and mustard. Every part matters. The bread should be a medium-sliced white loaf, not too thin, not artisan sourdough. The butter goes on both slices. The English mustard should be assertive enough to cut through the fat of the ham. And the ham must be thick-cut and good: wafer-thin deli ham compressed into a plastic packet is a different food entirely.

items.prepNote: thick-cut, from a joint or quality deli

content.text: Lay out {{bread-white}} slices of bread. Spread all four slices generously with {{salted-butter}} of soft salted butter, right to the edges.
Spread {{english-mustard}} of English mustard on one buttered side of each pair. Use more or less depending on how strong you want the heat.
Divide {{ham-cooked}} of ham between the mustard-covered slices, folded to fill the bread. Close the sandwiches and press firmly.
Cut diagonally and serve immediately, or wrap in wax paper and eat within 2 hours.

rows.cause: Mustard applied too far ahead or bread too thin
rows.fix: Use medium-sliced bread, not thin. Assemble no more than 2 hours ahead. Butter acts as a barrier between the bread and the mustard.

rows.cause: Too much ham or slices not folded
rows.fix: Fold the ham slices to match the size of the bread. Pack it flat rather than stacked high.

rows.symptom: Mustard is too hot to eat
rows.cause: English mustard is much stronger than French or wholegrain
rows.fix: Start with half a teaspoon per sandwich and add more after tasting. English mustard is strongest mustard in common British use.

rows.symptom: Sandwich tastes flat despite good ham
rows.cause: Butter at fridge temperature, applied too thin
rows.fix: Soft butter at room temperature spreads to the edges and coats the bread properly. Cold butter tears the bread and leaves gaps.

content.text: The ham sandwich is the most basic entry in the British sandwich tradition that dates formally from the 1760s, when John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, reportedly ate cold meat between slices of bread at the gaming table to avoid interrupting a game. Whether the story is true or not, the sandwich became associated with his name, and the bread-and-filling format spread rapidly. Ham and mustard became one of the standard filling combinations across British catering, from school lunch boxes to station buffets to office cafeterias. It is what a British ham sandwich looks like: thick ham, mustard, white bread, butter. No extras.
